# ERYSIPELAS

In contrast to cellulitis, erysipelas has sharply demarcated borders and a characteristic raised, orange-peel appearance. Most cases are associated with streptococcus. In a minority of cases, especially those involving the face, Staphylococcus aureus is also a potential pathogen. In severe cases, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage must be provided until microbiology results are available.
Treat for 5 to 10days, longer if patient is bacteremic.

---

## Facial

---

Sudden onset of rapidly spreading red edematous tender plaque-like skin on the face in an otherwise healthy host.

[References](references)
Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59: 147
Sanford keyword: Erysipelas
Mandell chapter: Cellulitis and subcutaneous tissue infections Up-to-Date website
Therapy:
## Inpatient

### If erysipelas-like on the face treat as if MRSA is present:

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]

### Non-facial

### MILD TO MODERATE disease

Penicillin VK 250 - 500 mg PO q6h ($) [R]

### Alternative for penicillin allergy

Erythromycin 500 mg po q6h ($) [DI]

### SEVERE disease

Penicillin 3 million units IV q6h ($) [R]

### Alternative for penicillin allergy or MRSA suspected

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
< OR >
Clindamycin 600 mg IV q8h ($) [H,O]

## Outpatient

### If erysipelas-like on the face treat as if MRSA is present:

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

### Non-facial

### MILD TO MODERATE disease

Penicillin VK 250 - 500 mg PO QID for 10 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above

### Alternative for penicillin allergy

Erythromycin 250-500 mg PO QID ($) [DI]
Non-VA order for above

### SEVERE disease

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.
